en: The *Parinirvāṇa Sūtra*, Volume One;
the translator’s name is not recorded, appended to the Catalogue of the Eastern Jin.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Vulture Peak near Rājagṛha, accompanied by a great assembly of bhikṣus.
There were one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus at that time.
King Ajātaśatru of Magadha was at odds with the Vṛjis, and his ministers deliberated, saying:
"The Vṛjis rely on their own wealth and numerous population; their land is fertile and abundant, producing many rare treasures. Since they do not submit to us, we should go and attack them."
The state’s eminent minister was named Vṛṣṇa, of the Brahmin caste.

The king commanded him to go and, bowing his head at the Buddha’s feet, respectfully inquire after his well-being, asking whether he was free from ailment, strong in spirit, and able to walk about, and whether his virtuous transformation was flourishing daily. He then said:
“Ajaśatru and the Vaijikas harbor a grievance; according to the deliberations of the ministers, we wish to go and wage war against them.”
"I pray that the World-Honored One will grant me instruction.

The minister received his orders and immediately prepared five hundred chariots, with two thousand cavalrymen and two thousand infantrymen. He set out for Vulture Peak; upon reaching the mouth of a small path, he alighted from his carriage and proceeded on foot. Seeing the Buddha, he was filled with joy; with a reverent countenance and respectful words, he performed a deep bow of courtesy. Having finished his salutations, he knelt down and said:

"King Ajātaśatru of Magadha bows his head at the Buddha’s feet and respectfully inquires after your well-being, asking whether you are light in movement and strong in vigor as you walk about, and whether your virtuous transformation is flourishing day by day."
The Buddha said, "Excellent!
Are you, the king, the people of the country, and yourself all at peace?
Vṛṣṭika replied:

"The King harbors a grievance against the Yue-zhi. After consultation among the ministers, it was decided that because they rely on their own wealth, large population, fertile lands, abundant harvests, and great production of rare treasures, they have not submitted to us; we wish to go and attack them."
"I wish to hear the Buddha's teaching.
The Buddha replied to the minister:

"In the past, on one occasion, I traveled to the abode of the deity Zhengzao in the kingdom of Vaiśālī. I saw that the people of that land were for the most part conscientious and diligent. At that time, I preached to them the Way of the Seven Dharmas for Governing a State so as not to Fall into Peril. Those who are able to practice these will see their state flourish daily and never decline."
He then joined his palms and said:
"I wish to hear of the seven dharmas; what, indeed, should be practiced?
The Buddha said:
"Listen attentively.
They replied,
"We receive your instruction."
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda was standing behind the Buddha fanning him.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Have you not heard how the people of the kingdom of Vaiśālī frequently gather together to discuss matters of state and maintain their defenses?"
He replied,
“I have heard that they gather together in numbers to discuss matters of state and prepare themselves for self-defense.
The Buddha said:

"In this way, he shall not decline. You have heard that the ruler and ministers of Vaiśālī are always in harmony, that those they employ are loyal and virtuous, and that they succeed one another in office.
He replied, "I have heard that their ruler and ministers are always in harmony, that those they employ are loyal and virtuous, and that they succeed one another in office."
"Have you heard that the people of Vaiśālī follow the Dharma together, being without grasping or desire, and not daring to commit transgressions? He replied,
"I have heard that they follow the Dharma together, being without grasping or desire, and not daring to commit transgressions."
“Have you heard that the people of Vaiśālī are refined in their customs and reverent, with distinct roles for men and women, and that elders and juniors serve one another? He replied,
“I have heard that their customs are refined and reverent, with distinct roles for men and women, and that elders and juniors serve one another.”
“Have you heard that the people of Vaiśālī are filial toward their parents and respectful toward their teachers and elders, receiving and acknowledging their instructions?
He replied,
“I have heard that they are filial toward their parents and respectful toward their teachers and elders, receiving and acknowledging their instructions.”
“Have you heard that the people of Vaiśālī follow the patterns of heaven and earth, revere ghosts and spirits, and respectfully accord with the four seasons? He replied,
“I have heard that they follow the patterns of heaven and earth, revere ghosts and spirits, and respectfully accord with the four seasons.”

“Have you heard that in Vaiśālī they honor the Way and its virtue, and that there are śramaṇas who are arhats, as well as those coming from the four quarters, whom they provide with clothing, food, bedding, and medicine for the sick?”

He replied, "I have heard that he reveres the Way and its Virtue; that there are śramaṇas, arhats, and those who come from the four quarters within his kingdom, whom he provides with clothing, food, bedding, and medicine for the sick."
The Buddha said,
"One who rules a kingdom and practices these seven dharmas will find it difficult to be endangered. Vṛṣa replied:
"If the people of Vaiśālī were to possess even one of these, they would still be unassailable; how much more so with seven?
There are many affairs of state, so I must return.
Thus he took his leave.
The Buddha said, "Very well;
you may go, knowing that this is the proper time.
He then rose from his seat, paid homage to the Buddha, and departed.
At that time, the Buddha commanded the Venerable Ānanda to invite all the bhikṣus practicing solitary meditation on Mount Śyena to assemble in the lecture hall.
They were immediately invited and gathered; having bowed their heads in prostration, they sat down to one side.
The Buddha told them: "O bhikṣus!
Listen to my words and practice them with careful mindfulness."
They all replied,
“We shall receive your instruction.
The Buddha said:
“Monks, if there are seven teachings, the Dharma will not decline.
What are these seven teachings?
First, one should regularly assemble to lecture upon and recite the sutras and the Way, without any indolence.”
Second, they should be harmonious and compliant, instructing one another with loyalty and integrity, and successively transmitting and practicing these teachings.
Third, they should have no acquisitiveness or desires toward others, finding joy only in the mountains and marshes.
Fourth, they should sever all expectations regarding seniority and precedence among the young and old, serving one another according to the rites.
Fifth, one should practice loving-kindness and filial piety in serving teachers and elders, receiving and internalizing their instructions.
Sixth, one should revere the Dharma, stand in awe of the sutras and precepts, and thereby cultivate the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
Seventh, one should follow the Way in making offerings to the noble assembly, enlightening the ignorant, and providing clothing, food, bedding, and medicine for those who come to study.
With these seven dharmas, the teaching may endure for a long time.
Furthermore, when a bhikṣu possesses seven forms of guarding, the Dharma will not decline; he should practice them with right mindfulness:
first, guarding purity by taking no delight in conditioned phenomena.
Second, maintain freedom from desire, not coveting gain or offerings.
Third, maintain patience, remaining free from contention or dispute.
Fourth, maintain the practice of emptiness, not entering into crowds or assemblies.
Fifth, maintain the intention of guarding the precepts so that no manifold thoughts arise.
Sixth, maintain a single mind, sitting in dhyāna with a concentrated mind.
Seventh, maintain frugality and austerity, using coarse clothing and food, and making a bed of grass and straw.
"These seven dharmas can ensure that the teaching remains long-lasting.
Furthermore, if bhikṣus possess seven forms of reverence, the Dharma will not decline; they should practice them with mindful reflection:
first, they should revere the Buddha, serving him with a virtuous mind and acting without dependence on anything else."
Second is to revere the Dharma, setting one's will upon the aspiration for enlightenment and practicing without relying on anything else.
Third is to revere the Sangha, following and receiving their instructions and commands, and practicing without relying on anything else.
Fourth is to honor study, serving those who uphold the precepts without relying on anything else.
Fifth is to honor learning, serving those who expound and transmit the teachings without relying on anything else.
Sixth is reverent purity and freedom from desire, practicing without dependence on anything else.
Seventh is reverent concentration, engaging in the practice of seated meditation and tranquility, practicing without dependence on anything else.
Through these seven dharmas, one may abide for a long time.
"Furthermore, when a bhikṣu possesses the seven treasures, the Dharma will not decline; he should practice with right mindfulness:
first, he must have faith, seeing the truth and rejoicing in it;
second, he must have precepts, guarding them with care so as not to transgress; third, he must have a sense of shame, reforming his errors and repenting of himself."
Fourth, one should possess a sense of shame and act in accordance with one’s words.
Fifth, one should be widely learned, reciting and chanting without weariness.
Sixth, one should possess wisdom and practice the profound and subtle.
Seventh, one should practice the gift of Dharma without expecting gifts or honors in return.
Through these seven dharmas, the Teaching may endure for a long time.
Furthermore, when a bhikṣu possesses the seven factors of awakening, the Dharma will not decline; he should practice them with right mindfulness:
First, the awakening factor of mindfulness relies on purity and freedom from lust, abandoning distracted thoughts.
Second, the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena relies on purity and freedom from lust, abandoning distracted thoughts.
Third, the awakening factor of energy relies on purity and freedom from lust, abandoning distracted thoughts.
4. The awakening factor of joy relies on purity and freedom from lust;
it abandons distracted thoughts. 5. The awakening factor of rapture relies on purity and freedom from lust;
it abandons distracted thoughts. 6. The awakening factor of concentration relies on purity and freedom from lust; it abandons distracted thoughts.
The seven modes of conduct for guarding the awakening factors—relying on purity and freedom from lust, and abandoning distracted thoughts—these seven dharmas enable one to abide for a long time.
Furthermore, when a bhikṣu possesses seven knowledges, the Dharma will not decline; he should practice them with right mindfulness:
First, one should know the Dharma: to receive, recite, and discuss the twelve divisions of the Buddha’s scriptures with earnestness.
Second, one should know the analysis: to seek the wisdom of all dharmas and extensively understand their essential points.
Third, one should know the proper time: when to recite, when to walk, when to meditate, and when to lie down, never missing the appropriate occasion.
Fourth, one should know for oneself the extent and depth of the Dharma-practice entered, whether it is mature or at its inception, and one’s resolve should be ever more excellent.
Fifth, one should know moderation: do not covet what is exquisite; eat with moderation so as to suit the body, lest you bring illness upon yourself.

Sixth, one should know the assembly: when entering the assembly of bhikṣus, brahmins, sages, gentlemen, and common people, one should distinguish those who are worthy of respect, those with whom one may dwell, those with whom one may sit, those with whom one may remain silent, and those with whom one may speak.

Seventh, one should know how to observe the inclinations of people and examine their aspirations and abilities, then provide guidance according to their dispositions so that they may understand the transformation of the Sage.
Through these seven methods, the Dharma can endure for a long time.
"Furthermore, there are seven contemplations by which a bhikṣu shall not let the Dharma decline; he should practice them with right mindfulness:

First, contemplate the Way of the Sūtras as one contemplates one's parents. While parents give birth to a child and their concern lasts only for a single lifetime, the Dharma sustains people and delivers beings from birth and death through countless lifetimes."

Second, reflect that in human life there is no one who does not experience suffering. One should consider the wife, family members, and all possessions; at death, each will be separated and scattered, and one will not know where they have fallen. If the body has committed transgressions, even close kin cannot resolve them. Knowing this impermanence, one should mindfully practice the Path.
Third, one must be diligent and refined, rectifying body, speech, and mind; thus, attaining the Way will not be difficult.

Fourth, one must be humble and modest, without self-conceit or arrogance; one should serve those who are wise and enlightened, seeking instruction on what has not yet been heard, and regarding them with compassion as they teach.
Fifth, contemplate lowering the mind so as not to let the six sense-faculties run wild; suppress the states of lust, anger, and delusion, and remain free from deviant conduct.
Sixth, contemplate the body within: it contains nothing but foul impurities—wind, cold, heat, and blood—and there is nothing therein worth craving.

Seventh, contemplate yourself alone: your form is like excrement or soil. You should daily reflect on death; from the opening of heaven and earth until the birth of the people, there has been no one who did not die. This world is like a dream; regarding those whom you see as joyful and beloved, you do not realize they are illusory transformations. Only upon awakening do you perceive their emptiness; you should know them to be phantoms and must not deceive yourself.
"These seven dharmas can ensure that [the teaching] endures for a long time.
Furthermore, there are six further dharmas of gravity which a bhikṣu should practice with careful mindfulness; thus they may endure for a long time:

first, the cultivation of the body, by which one gives rise to a mind of loving-kindness, relies upon the noble penetrations, and as one of those who are pure, undertakes this heavy responsibility, harmonizing with affection and respect, bestowing it upon his fellow students, being without grasping or contention, and striving together to maintain the practice."
Second, to cultivate virtuous conduct of speech by giving rise to a mind of loving-kindness.
Third, to cultivate virtuous conduct of mind by giving rise to a mind of loving-kindness.
Fourth, regarding the limit of all phenomena as perceived: if one obtains clothing, food, a bowl, or other requisites, one shall never cherish them or store them away.
Fifth is upholding the precepts without transgression, not bartering them away, and being able to exhort others to do the same.

Sixth is that, having emerged from right view through the essential gate of deliverance, one attains the knowledge and vision of the exhaustion of suffering and transcendence; performing this great responsibility with the pure application of the noble path, using harmony and loving respect toward fellow practitioners, being without grasping or contention, mutually supporting one another, and together maintaining the practice of the Way.

Furthermore, bhikṣus, you should feel compassion for all wriggling creatures, down to the lice and fleas, and must certainly apply a mind of loving-kindness toward them. When a person dies, you should grieve for them; though they have attained human birth, if they do not hear the Way, their family weeps and wails, yet they themselves do not know where their soul and spirit are headed.
Only those who have attained the Way can know this.

For this reason, the Buddha has expounded the teachings of the sutras; these sutras must be studied, and the Way must be practiced. Although there are many paths in the world, the Royal Way is the greatest; the Buddha-way is likewise so, being the most supreme of all.

It is like ten people shooting at a target together: some hit it first, others hit it later, yet as long as they do not cease shooting, they will surely hit the target again; it is also like the myriad streams of the world, which flow incessantly and all return to the sea.

In this way, monks, if you practice the Path without ceasing, you will surely attain liberation. Following the teachings of the Buddha, transmit them to one another; recite the words of the Buddha and constantly use them to instruct others. Let the fourfold assembly of disciples teach one another in turn; in this manner, the Buddha’s sutras shall endure for a long time.
At that time, the Buddha invited the venerable Ānanda to go together to Pāṭaliputra; he immediately accepted the instruction and set out.
The Buddha took up his robe and bowl and, passing through Rājagṛha, traveled halfway along the road before stopping at the King’s Garden.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

"Listen all of you! Those who practice the Way must know the Four Noble Truths. Because ordinary people do not know them, they wander upon the long road, revolving through birth and death without a moment's rest; it is for this reason that I have explained this meaning to you."
What are the four?
First is the knowledge that suffering is suffering; this is called a noble truth.
Second is that suffering arises from its origin; this is called a noble truth.
Third is the cessation of the origin of suffering; this is called a noble truth.
Fourth is the path leading to the cessation of the origin of suffering; this is called a noble truth.
Because one lacks wisdom regarding suffering and does not understand it, one wanders along the long road of saṃsāra without rest; therefore, one must come to know this Truth of Suffering.

Suffering refers to the suffering of birth, the suffering of old age, the suffering of illness, the suffering of death, the suffering of grief, lamentation, pain, and despair, the suffering of separation from what is loved, and the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks;
in brief, it is the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging.

Having already awakened to this suffering and being able to sever the habituation to craving, this is called "attaining the eye. This is the final birth; thereafter there will be no further suffering.

Just as those who habituate follow from craving, when the accumulation of suffering is completely exhausted, one receives the Truth of the Path, attains the eye, and realizes it through direct witness; this is the end of this birth, and thereafter there will be no further existence.
Having seen the True Realities and attained the Eye of the Path, one no longer undergoes birth and death; the long journey is forever severed.
Thus, O Bhikṣu, you should further know that the attainment of the Path consists of eight practices.
What are the eight?
First, with a focused mind, receive the Buddha’s sutras and teachings.
Second, abandon craving and desire, and remain without contention with the world.
Third, one shall never engage in killing, stealing, or sexual misconduct.
Fourth, one shall not practice deception, slander, flattery, or malicious abuse.
Fifth, one shall not harbor jealousy, greed, gluttony, or lack of faith.
Sixth, one contemplates impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self.
Seventh, one contemplates the foulness and impurity within the physical form.
Eighth, one does not crave the body, knowing that it must return to the earth.

All Buddhas of the past have seen these Four Truths; all Buddhas of the future shall likewise see these Four Truths. Those who harbor longing for domestic life and its endearments, or who delight in worldly fame and longevity, will ultimately never attain this path that transcends the world.
The Way arises from the mind; only those whose minds are pure attain the Way.
Next, those whose minds are upright and who do not violate the five precepts may ascend to heaven;
next, those who believe in the Way and delight in studying the scriptures and the Dharma may later become human beings again.
If you wish to completely sever the paths of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts, you should, with a single mind, uphold and practice the sutras and precepts.
Now the Buddha, for the sake of the world, has explained liberation from birth and death and revealed the Right Path; those who wish to study it should contemplate it with careful attention.
The Buddha and the Venerable Ānanda proceeded to Pāṭaliputra and stayed beneath a sacred tree outside the city.

When the brahmins and householders heard that the Buddha had arrived with his disciples, they all went out of the city, desiring to visit and make offerings to the Buddha. Some carried mats and grass seats; some carried woolen rugs; some carried water and refreshments, as well as oil lamps. They went to where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves, and sat to one side.
The Buddha addressed the brahmins and householders:
"When a person lives in the world and is fond of greed and indulgence, there are five forms of depletion:
first, by being self-indulgent, one's wealth and property diminish daily."
Second, by indulging in self-indulgence, one endangers one's life and loses the Way.
Third, by indulging in self-indulgence, people will not respect one, and one will have regrets at the time of death.
Fourth, by indulging in self-indulgence, one’s ugliness and ill repute will spread throughout the world.
If one indulges in the five forms of self-indulgence, at death the soul shall fall into the three evil realms;
yet if a person can subdue the mind and does not indulge, there are five abundant virtues:
first, by exercising self-restraint, one's wealth and property increase daily.
Second, by exercising self-restraint, one draws near to the aspiration for the Way.
Third, by exercising self-restraint, one is honored by the multitude and remains without regret until death.
Fourth, by exercising self-restraint, one’s good reputation and virtuous fame spread throughout the world.
"Fifth is self-restraint: when the body dies, one is reborn in heaven, a land of merit.
If a person does not indulge themselves and possesses these five virtues, they should reflect upon them.

The Buddha preached this Dharma for the assembly with various essential words of true transformation; there was none who did not rejoice. They all came forward, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times, and departed.
Thereupon, the Buddha rose and went to Āpāpā, where he sat beneath a tree. With his divine mind and the eye of the Way, he beheld the higher devas and commanded the noble spirits to guard this place.
The venerable Ānanda rose from his meditation, prostrated himself, and stood to one side.
The Buddha asked Ānanda,
"Who is planning to build the city walls for this Pāṭaliputra?"
He replied,
"This was built by Varsakāra, the minister of Magadha, with the intent to block the advance of the Vaijikas.
The Buddha said:
“Excellent! Excellent!
The worthy Vṛṣabha has indeed understood how to plan this.”
I have seen that the various wondrous devas of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven together sustain this land; wherever there is territory protected by celestial deities, it will surely be peaceful and noble.

Furthermore, as for this land, it is situated near the heavens, and the presiding deity of this land is named Manuṣyadatta (Human-Intent). Protected by Manuṣyadatta, that kingdom will flourish for a long time and become increasingly superior, inevitably producing many sages, worthies, benevolent and wise men, and eminent talents, such that other nations cannot equal it, nor can they ever destroy it.
After this city has existed for a long time, when it is on the verge of destruction, it shall be ruined by three things:
first, a great fire; second, a great flood; and third, the internal inhabitants conspiring with outsiders.

When Vṛṣaśarman heard that the Buddha, together with his assembly of disciples, had arrived there on his travels, he immediately mounted five hundred royal state carriages and went out of the city, desiring to visit and make offerings to the Buddha.

Upon arrival, he alighted from his carriage and entered the garden gate on foot. Seeing the Buddha, he was filled with joy; with a reverent countenance and respectful words, he exchanged profound salutations and withdrew to sit to one side.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for him, providing various essential instructions of true transformation. Vṛṣabha was delighted and, rising from his seat, said: "I wish to provide a modest meal;
I pray that you and the assembly of noble ones will deign to accept my invitation."
The Buddha signaled his consent by remaining silent.
The minister immediately rose, prostrated himself, circumambulated the Buddha three times, and returned home.
Upon his arrival, he spent the entire night preparing excellent food and decorating the hall, arranging couches and seats within.
He went early to inform the Buddha, saying, "The meal is prepared; may the Holy One know the time.

The Buddha then adjusted his robes, took up his bowl, and together with his assembly of disciples, arrived at the house. He took his place on the high seat before the assembly. Varṣākāra personally served the exquisite food, presented the bowls, and offered the gruel. After the water for washing was finished, he stood and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"By the merit of what has been given, may the Buddha offer his blessing so that all the people and officials of this land, as well as all devas and humans, may long enjoy peace.
The Buddha offered this blessing, saying: "The Buddha rejoices in your joy.

Having made offerings to the devas and humans, acting as a guide for the people of the land, providing food for the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus, praising the True Dharma, receiving the words of the wisdom of the Path, and practicing the sutras and precepts—I bless you all with this: may you respect those worthy of respect and serve those worthy of service; may you practice extensive giving and universal love, possessing a heart of compassion; and may you always obtain benefit and merit, and attain the vision of the Right Path."
The minister was filled with joy, and the Buddha spoke again:
"Although you have official duties in this present life, by virtue of this merit, you will surely attain liberation in the future."
If a person obtains food and offers it to the Buddha and to those who are truly virtuous and uphold the precepts, and the śramaṇas offer prayers of blessing, it shall never be in vain.

Furthermore, you should know that if one wishes to hold office or occupy a position of authority, one must not harbor a greedy mind, a luxurious mind, a haughty mind, a cruel mind, or a self-indulgent mind. By abandoning these five states of mind, one will later be free from reproach and regret; upon death, one will ascend to heaven and be cleared of the sins of the evil realms.
After the Buddha had finished speaking, he rose from his seat and departed through the eastern city gate.
Vṛṣa followed in attendance, saying, "This gate shall be named the Gautama Gate.
When the Buddha crossed a ford, Vṛṣa again followed him and named it the Gautama Ford.
At that time, among the people, some crossed by means of large boats, some by small boats, and others by bamboo rafts or wooden floats; those who crossed were exceedingly numerous.
The Buddha sat in meditative concentration and reflected to himself:
"In the past, before I became a Buddha, the number of times my body traveled upon this raft cannot be counted;
now that I have attained liberation, I shall no longer ride it, and I shall cause all my disciples to be free from it as well."
The Buddha arose from his meditative absorption and spoke these verses himself:
"The Buddha is the captain of the ocean-going ship; The Dharma is the bridge across the river’s ford.
The scriptures of the Mahāyāna path Carry all devas and humans across."
"He has also brought about his own liberation, crossed to the further shore, and attained the state of the Immortal;
he has caused all his disciples to untie their bonds and reach Nirvāṇa.
At that time, the Buddha invited the Venerable Ānanda to go together to the village of Kuḷī, and they both set out accordingly, arriving and sitting beneath a tree.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
“Listen all!
You should maintain pure precepts, cultivate concentrated mind, and realize the practice of wisdom.”

These three—having already achieved great renown through meditation and having further attained liberation from the defilements of lust, anger, and delusion—are called the swift and correct crossing over desire.

Anticipating this, one should strive to liberate oneself, exhausting this present life and entering into pure conduct. One must apply oneself to what ought to be done, maintain single-mindedness, and cultivate one's nature. Remaining without contention with the world and having understood worldly affairs, one should take concern for oneself alone, dwelling in stillness and reflecting inwardly. When the will becomes clear and the three defilements are eliminated, one will spontaneously attain the Way.

The mind no longer wanders and has nothing to which it clings; just as a king is the sovereign of the myriad people, so too does a bhikṣu reflect that he can manage all matters, yet the mind is the sovereign of them all.
The Buddha, together with Ānanda, arrived at the town of Xiyu and stayed by the riverbank beneath a *kaṇikāra* tree.
While the disciples entered the city to beg for food, they returned after finishing their ablutions to pay homage to the Buddha. Standing before him, they addressed the Buddha, saying:

"This country has suffered much from pestilence, and there have been those who died, as we heard together this morning. Among them were the lay devotees Xuantan, Shixian, Chudong, Huozhen, Shuliang, Kuaxian, Bozong, Jiandu, Decheng, and Jinggao—ten men in all—who have all passed away. When these individuals lose their bodies, to which realm will they go?"
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"These ten persons have already severed their natural soul-spirits and been reborn above in the eighteen heavens of the form realm, reaching the stage of non-returning (anāgāmin); they shall no longer descend again to undergo the dharmas of the world."
Furthermore, those who die in this land are not limited to these alone.

With his divine eye, the Buddha saw that five hundred lay devotees (upāsakas), all like Nandika, were equally free from the three impurities; having severed the cycle of death within the five realms of existence, they had all been reborn in the stage of Non-returner (anāgāmin) and would there attain Nirvāṇa.

Furthermore, there were three hundred laymen of pure faith who had severed the three fetters, were free from lust, anger, and delusion, and had ascended to the stage of Once-returners; having returned for one more birth, they shall reach the end of suffering.

Furthermore, there were five hundred female lay devotees who had all attained the four joys; with the three fetters exhausted, they had entered the stream, departed from the three evil realms, and would be reborn among gods and humans, attaining arhatship within no more than seven lifetimes.
Thereupon the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"You who speak of that dead man are merely troubling me.
However, as I am a Buddha, I no longer undergo such things; why then should I fear?"
How subtle and wondrous!
Birth and death have their appointed times; when the Buddhas arise, although they are said to be born into the world, they do not harbor worldly sentiments. Why is this so?
The Tathāgata’s dharma-feeling has already ceased; there is nothing he does not perceive. Having fully understood this birth, he now explains it clearly.

That which is called "wondrous" means: from the existence of this, that is obtained; where this does not exist, that is not obtained. From the arising of this, that is produced; when this ceases, that is utterly extinguished.

Why is this so? Because there is the seeking of desire, there is ignorance (*avidyā*); conditioned by ignorance are volitional formations (*saṃskāra*); conditioned by volitional formations is consciousness (*vijñāna*); conditioned by consciousness are name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*); conditioned by name-and-form are the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*); conditioned by the six sense bases is contact (*sparśa*); conditioned by contact is feeling (*vedanā*); conditioned by feeling is craving (*tṛṣṇā*); conditioned by craving is grasping (*upādāna*); conditioned by grasping is becoming (*bhava*); conditioned by becoming is birth (*jāti*); and conditioned by birth come old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. Thus is the accumulation of the nature of suffering brought to fulfillment; it is the root of birth and death, revolving like a wheel, proceeding without rest.

From ignorance and lack of clarity comes birth and death; if one were to extinguish this ignorance through the absence of remainder and desire, then volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) would cease. With the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness (*vijñāna*) ceases; with the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) ceases; with the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) cease; with the cessation of the six sense bases, contact (*sparśa*) ceases; with the cessation of contact, sensation (*vedanā*) ceases; with the cessation of sensation, craving (*tṛṣṇā*) ceases; with the cessation of craving, grasping (*upādāna*) ceases; with the cessation of grasping, becoming (*bhava*) ceases; with the cessation of becoming, birth (*jāti*) ceases; and with the cessation of birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, dejection, and despair cease. Thus, the entire mass of suffering, the conditioned nature of existence, is completely extinguished.
Therefore, I have previously explained to you that the deluded undergo birth and death, while the wise uphold the Path and no longer undergo birth and death.
You should reflect upon this; by subduing your mind, you will not uphold the path of further birth and death.
Furthermore, one who wishes to draw near to the Way should possess four kinds of joy and should practice them with right mindfulness:
first, mindfulness of the Buddha, maintaining joyful intent without separation;
second, mindfulness of the Dharma, maintaining joyful intent without separation.
The third is mindfulness of the Sangha, with a mind of joy that never departs from it.
The fourth is mindfulness of the precepts, with a mind of joy that never departs from them.

One must ensure that these four forms of joy are fully perfected and clearly realized for oneself; one should aspire to Right Crossing and seek the essential liberation of the body, thereby severing the paths of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts, attaining the stage of Stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*), and no longer falling into evil realms. Although one may still wander between the heavens and the human world, after no more than seven births, one will naturally reach the end of suffering.
At that time, the Buddha invited the Venerable Ānanda to go together to the kingdom of Vaiśālī; he immediately accepted the instruction and set out.
The Buddha traveled through the city of Koliya with delight, and upon arriving outside the city, he stayed there, looking toward the grove of Āmrapālī.

When the lady Nai heard that the Buddha had come from Vaiśālī with his disciples, she immediately prepared her carriage and attire and, accompanied by five hundred female disciples, went out of the city to the Nai Garden to prostrate herself, attend upon him, and pay her respects.
The Buddha saw the five hundred women approaching from afar and commanded the bhikṣus:

"See them all; you should lower your heads and look within, straightening your own minds. Their fine garments and ornaments are like painted jars: though the exterior displays brilliant colors, the interior contains nothing but excrement and urine. You should know that these beautiful women are all of the same sort as painted jars."

Now, one who practices the Way should not be deluded by external things; therefore, they must exercise firm self-mastery, their resolve being solely on discernment. Even if you come toward me, you shall likewise follow my teaching.
What is meant by "firm restraint"?
It is the ability to immediately sever evil dharmas that have already arisen, exercising vigor in one's nature and maintaining self-restraint over the mind;
it is the ability to prevent evil dharmas that have not yet arisen from arising, exercising vigor in one's nature and maintaining self-restraint over the mind.
Regarding wholesome states that have not yet arisen, the mind is able to bring them forth; this is the cultivation of energetic effort through self-restraint and mental rectitude.

Regarding wholesome states that have already arisen, one establishes the will so as not to forget them, enabling them to increase and expand; this is the cultivation of energetic effort through self-restraint and mental rectitude.
Therefore, one should act in such a way that one would rather break one's sinews and bones, or shatter one's own body, than follow the mind to commit evil; this is called "vigorous restraint.
What is meant by "resolute reflection"?

One contemplates the body within as the body, one contemplates the body without as the body; through such internal and external contemplation, one reflects with discernment to sever and not allow the mind to proliferate.

One contemplates feelings within as feelings, one contemplates feelings without as feelings; through such internal and external contemplation, one reflects with discernment to sever and not allow the mind to proliferate.

One contemplates the mind within as the mind, one contemplates the mind without as the mind; through such internal and external contemplation, one reflects with discernment to sever and not allow the mind to proliferate.

One contemplates internal phenomena according to the Dharma, contemplates external phenomena according to the Dharma, and through such internal and external contemplation, one reflects and discerns to sever [defilements] so as not to allow them to influence the mind;
this is called the application of mindfulness to intention.
What is meant by "discriminating knowledge of what is practicable and what is impracticable"?
To be able to distinguish between right and wrong actions is what constitutes discrimination.
One who is capable of firmly restraining their will and exercising such discrimination is truly powerful; it is not merely a strong man with great physical strength who is called powerful.
To be able to abandon evil and pursue good is called being most courageous.

Since I began seeking Buddhahood and contending with my own mind, countless eons have passed; because I did not listen to my deviant mind, I have now attained Buddhahood for the sake of the world and may now rest. Your mind has long remained within impurity; you should pull yourself out and escape these manifold sufferings.
"When you see this woman approaching, you must act according to my instructions.
Thereupon, the daughter of the Naga arrived; having prostrated herself, she sat to one side.
The Buddha asked her, "Now, what is the intention of you daughters?"
He replied, "Having received the Buddha’s great kindness and been able to hear his teachings, my ignorance has been awakened; day and night I admonish myself, not daring to harbor an evil mind."
The Buddha told the daughter of Nanda:
"One who delights in sexual misconduct has five self-inflicted hindrances:
first, their voice becomes harsh and unpleasant."
Second, they will be afflicted by the laws of the king;
third, they will harbor heterodox views and be full of doubt;
fourth, after death, they will enter hell.
Fifth, after the retribution for hellish offenses is exhausted, one receives the form of an animal;
all such states are brought about by one's own actions, yet one can extinguish the mind through self-effort.
For one who refrains from sexual misconduct, there are five increases in merit:
First, one is praised by many people;
second, one does not fear local officials;
third, one attains peace and security for oneself.
Fourth is rebirth among the devas after death;
fifth is the establishment of the path to pure nirvāṇa.

Therefore, one should cultivate weariness toward [this world]: being born of a mother, suffering from illness, the impurity of the menstrual cycle, being bound by fetters and beaten with whips, and lacking self-mastery. By receiving and practicing the sūtras and precepts, one may attain the pure path of a Buddha.
The Buddha taught the Dharma to the daughter of Naï with various essential instructions for her correct transformation. Delighted, the daughter of Naï rose from her seat, knelt down, and said:
"I wish to offer a modest meal; I pray that the Buddha and the assembly of noble ones will deign to accept my invitation."
The Buddha signaled his consent by remaining silent, whereupon [the Licchavis] prostrated and departed.

Not long after they had left, various Licchavis from the prominent clans of Vaiśālī heard that the Buddha was approaching with his disciples. Seven *li* from the city, they mounted their majestic four-colored royal chariots and set out, desiring to see the Buddha.
Among the Licchavis, some rode upon blue horses and blue chariots, with blue garments, blue canopies, blue banners, and blue pennants, while their attendants were all dressed in blue;
some rode upon yellow horses and yellow chariots, with yellow garments, yellow canopies, yellow banners, and yellow pennants, while their attendants were all dressed in yellow;
and some rode upon red horses and red chariots, with their garments, canopies, banners, and pennants, as well as their attendants, all being red.
There were those riding white horses in white chariots, with clothing, canopies, banners, and attendants all white.
Seeing hundreds of thousands of carriages and cavalry filling the road as they approached, the Buddha immediately addressed the bhikṣus:
"If you wish to see the attendants entering and exiting the celestial gardens of Śakra, Lord of the Devas, in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, it is no different from this."

When the Licchavis arrived, they all alighted from their vehicles and entered the Āmrapālī grove on foot. Having paid their respects, they sat to one side, and the Buddha taught the Dharma for the sake of the great assembly, providing them with correct instruction.
There was a man named Bingbian who rose from his seat to adjust his robes, approached the Buddha, and addressed him, saying:

"Whenever I hear of the Buddha’s merit, it is so lofty and vast that all within heaven and earth are moved by it. I have always followed wherever you were, revering and admiring you day and night; I submit to your profound and pure transformation and do not dare to cause you any disturbance."
The Buddha spoke again:

"The wise and sagacious of the world know how to revere the Buddha. Now, those who revere the Buddha shall naturally obtain blessings for themselves; upon death, they will all ascend to heaven and not fall into the evil realms."
Thereupon, together with his attendants, he spoke this verse in praise:
"I have come to pay my respects to the Dharma King; My mind is settled through the power of the Right Path.
The Most Victorious One is called Buddha; His fame is as manifest as the Snowy Mountains."
Like a pure flower, free from doubt, one attains joy as if drawing near to fragrance;
beholding his form, one never tires, for his radiance shines like dewdrops.
Only the Buddha’s wisdom is sublime and profound; its brilliance is full and untainted by the dust of defilement.
"I vow to uphold the precepts of pure faith and take refuge in the Triple Gem.

At that time, five hundred noblemen among those seated there each removed their upper garments and presented them to Piṇḍola. Holding the garments, Piṇḍola stepped forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"These venerable ones have rejoiced upon hearing these virtuous words; they have together offered these five hundred upper garments to the World-Honored One. I pray that you will compassionately accept them."
Having accepted it, the Buddha addressed him, saying: "Messenger,

you should know that when a Buddha appears in the world as a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed One, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, called Buddha and Bhagavat, there are five things that are difficult to find and yet occur naturally."
What are these five?

A Buddha appears to teach and transform the world; for Śakras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, brahmins, nāgas, spirits, kings, and emperors, he manifests realization for the sake of the world through his spontaneous wisdom, expounding the True Path. His words are excellent in the beginning, excellent in the middle, and excellent in the end; they are complete in their essential meaning, pure and thoroughly elucidated, and fully unfolded—all this is a spontaneous dharma that is difficult to encounter.

When the Buddha preached the sutras throughout the world, all who heard them rejoiced; they believed, studied, and recited them, rectifying their body, speech, and mind, abandoning the depraved and entering the correct path—these two are natural laws that are difficult to encounter.

When the people of the world hear the Way of the Buddha’s sutras, their minds are opened and liberated; through deep contemplation, they all attain clear wisdom—this is the natural law of that which is difficult to encounter.

When the people of the world hear the Buddha’s exhortations, many respond with love and reverence; they escape the three evil realms and are reborn among devas and humans, thereby attaining great benefit. This is the fourth natural law that is difficult to encounter.

When the people of the world hear the profound and subtle Dharma teachings of the Buddha’s Way, they understand the fundamental matters of the conditions of birth and death; severing their emotions and cutting off their desires, they all attain the path of liberation. Those with the first degree of diligence attain the Path of Arhatship (Sainthood); those with the second degree of diligence attain the Path of Non-returning; those with the third degree of diligence attain the Path of Once-returning; and those with the fourth degree of diligence attain the Path of Stream-entry. These five are the natural laws for those who encounter such rare opportunities.
If any person harbors a mind of devotion toward the Buddha and performs even a small act of merit through giving, they shall all obtain great blessings that will not go to waste.
Therefore, everyone, including those of low station, should exhort themselves to strive and learn how to attain this.
When the Buddha had finished speaking, the Licchavis rose from their seats, adjusted their robes, and with palms joined, said:
"We originally intended to invite the Buddha, but Nanda’s daughter has preempted us. We pray that you will accept our invitation for a later day; we have many affairs and wish now to take our leave."
The Buddha said,
"You should know the proper time. Thereupon,
they all prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times, and departed.
The daughter-in-law prepared rich and delicious food throughout the night, adorned the interior of the room, and at dawn, having arranged the seats, she went to inform the Buddha, saying:
"The meal is ready; may the Holy One know the time."
The Buddha, together with his assembly of disciples, arrived at her house and took his seat upon a high throne before the multitude.

The daughter of the Nai clan personally served him, offering the bowl and presenting the gruel; having completed the ritual of providing water for washing, she took a small stool and sat before the Buddha, wishing to inquire about the Dharma.
The Buddha said:

"If I were to act on your behalf in delighting in giving, you would later have no resentment or fear; you would gain much praise, your good reputation would increase daily, and all people would love and respect you. If a person can be free from stinginess, practicing benevolence and wisdom as their intelligence, they will thus be stainless and at peace, reborn among the devas in the heavens where they enjoy themselves with the various celestial beings."
The Buddha taught the Dharma to the daughter of Naya with various essential exhortations of correct transformation, and they were all filled with joy.
The Buddha then requested the Venerable Ānanda to go together to the town of Veṇugrāmaka, where they stayed beneath the trees in the grove to the north of the city.
In that year, the district of Zhufang suffered from famine, and the price of grain soared.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"There is a famine here, and it is difficult to obtain food through begging. You should divide yourselves into groups and travel separately to the various districts of Vaiśālī and Vṛji; thus you will not suffer from want."
Having received the instruction, he was about to depart when the Buddha said:

"Bhikṣu, you should know that you must harm yourself [by renouncing worldly concerns]: do not rejoice in obtaining the good, nor grieve in obtaining the bad. Take food only to sustain the body; do not greedily seek delicacies. It is solely because of sitting and craving flavors, and because of the pursuit of such desires, that birth and death are never severed."
"Indeed, one who knows how to restrain the body and can practice self-reduction may attain a concentrated mind.

The Buddha preached the Dharma for them with various essential words of correct transformation; they all departed with joy, paid homage to the Buddha, and each went their separate way to travel through various kingdoms and towns.
The Buddha went alone with Ānanda to the village of Vairaṃbī.
At that time, the Buddha’s body was afflicted by illness, and his entire frame was in pain.

The Buddha reflected that the pain was severe and that his disciples were not present; he thought that he should enter *parinirvāṇa* only when the assembly had gathered. Therefore, through the power of his own diligence despite this illness, he entered the concentration (*samādhi*) of non-attention to all perceptions. He contemplated this concentration of non-attention to all perceptions according to its true nature, and through this patient resolve, he himself attained the hearing [of the Dharma].
The venerable Ānanda rose from beneath a tree, approached the Buddha, prostrated himself, and stood to one side. He inquired after the Buddha’s health, saying:
"Is your illness abating?"
Hearing that the Holy Body was ill, I am truly filled with anxiety and fear; might the World-Honored One not wish to enter *nirvāṇa*?
I pray for your instruction regarding the assembly of disciples.
The Buddha replied to Ānanda:
"How could the Buddha be far removed from the assembly?

I am also constantly present within the community of bhikṣus. Whatever instructions and admonitions I ought to provide—whether concerning what has been previously taught or what shall be taught hereafter—all take place within the assembly. You need only apply yourselves with diligence and practice according to the sūtras."

When my illness first arose, my entire body was in extreme pain; I immediately contemplated the meditative concentration that is free from discursive thoughts. Because my mind did not cling to the illness, this was the essential core within my endurance.

Ānanda! The Dharma I have taught is complete in both its internal and external aspects. As the Buddha is the Teacher of the Dharma, there is nothing forgotten; regarding what ought to be practiced, you yourself are fully capable of knowing it.

I too have grown old; my age is now nearly eighty. My body is like an ancient chariot—neither firm nor strong. I have always taught that birth and death have their appointed time, and that there is no one who is born who does not come to an end.
At the very summit there is a heaven named Unconceivable Entry; its lifespan lasts eighty-four million kalpas, yet even there, death occurs.
Therefore, the Buddha arises and traverses the world, universally demonstrating the Great Way of Nirvana in order to sever the root of birth and death.
I now provide lamps for those who possess a body so that they may take refuge in the body, and lamps for the teaching of the Dharma so that the Dharma itself may take refuge [in itself].
What is meant by "lamp"?
What is meant by "taking refuge"?

This means to focus one's mind exclusively on the four foundations of mindfulness: first, mindfulness of the body; second, mindfulness of sensation; third, mindfulness of the mind; and fourth, mindfulness of phenomena. One should skillfully restrain discursive thoughts and sever them so that they do not arise. This is the lamp of instruction for all conditioned phenomena, and it is therein that one should take refuge.
I have already explained this at length; those who wish to understand it should practice the precepts of the Way with diligent application, ensuring they remain constant as always.
Those who take refuge in it and awaken to the path of the Buddha’s sutras are all children of the Buddha.

Now I have renounced the position of a Wheel-Turning King to become a Buddha for the sake of the world, out of concern to deliver beings from the three realms; you all should likewise take concern for yourselves and sever all suffering.

When the time for avoiding the rain had passed and his robes were mended, the Buddha invited the Venerable Ānanda to go together to Vaiśālī. Having received these instructions, he set out immediately.

Upon arriving, they stayed at the Monkey Park; after finishing their almsround, the Buddha washed his bowl and rinsed himself, then again accompanied by Ānanda, proceeded to the Ground of the Swift Deity.
The Buddha said, “Ānanda!
Vaiśālī is pleasant, and Vṛji is also pleasant; now, throughout this world, in the sixteen great nations and all their districts and towns, everything is pleasant.”
The River Hiraṇyavatī abounds in gold; the land of Jambudvīpa is adorned with five-colored paintings; and when people are born into this world, they take their longevity as their joy.

If a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī understands the four bases of psychic power (*catvāra ṛddhipādāḥ*), this constitutes the uprooting of suffering. By practicing them extensively, maintaining them in mind without forgetting, and according to their own wishes, they may attain immortality for more than an eon (*kalpa*).
Thus it is, Ānanda!

Having extensively practiced the four bases of spiritual power and maintained them with focused mindfulness without forgetfulness, the Tathāgata can remain for a kalpa or more, according to his own wish.

The Buddha repeated these words two or three times, yet at that time Ānanda’s mind was submerged in peripheral thoughts; obscured by Māra, he was dazed and failed to realize the truth, remaining silent and without reply.
The Buddha said,
"Ānanda! Go to the foot of a tree and contemplate within yourself with a tranquil mind."
He immediately accepted the instruction and sat down in one place.
At that time, Māra Pāpīyas came and said:
"The Buddha’s intention is free from desire; he may now enter parinirvāṇa. His teaching and exhortation are complete and finished; he may now pass into extinction."
In the past, when the Buddha was traveling along the Uruvilvā River, he explained to the elders, saying:
"Although I have attained mastery as a Buddha, I do not crave to dwell for long; this does not refer to the present."
"The beings to be delivered have also been finished; you may now enter parinirvāṇa. The Buddha replied to Pāpīyān:

"The reason I have reached this state but have not yet entered extinction is that I must wait until my assembly of bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs have all attained wisdom and are able to receive and apply the sūtras and precepts; until those who have not yet entered [the path] are exhorted and brought to completion as learners. Furthermore, I must wait until I have invited the upāsakas and upāsikās so that they may attain wisdom and receive and apply the sūtras and precepts; until those who have not yet entered do enter, and those who have received the Dharma reach completion."

"Pāpīyān, it is because I have waited for these four classes of disciples until they have all attained the meaning of the Dharma, teaching one another in turn, liberating the ignorant, and bringing their studies to completion; for this reason, I have not entered parinirvāṇa until now."
Māra said,
“The time for it to be fulfilled has already passed.
The Buddha said:
“Be silent; before long, after these three months have passed, the Tathāgata shall enter parinirvāṇa.
Māra’s heart was then gladdened, and he departed with joy.
The Buddha then sat upright and, concentrating his mind, reflected within himself:
"Within this samādhi, he does not abide in life or vitality, casting off all remaining life-functions.
At that moment, the earth shook greatly, the sky became pure, and the Buddha’s radiance shone forth boundlessly; the various devas came and filled the void on every side.
The Buddha arose from his meditative absorption and spoke these verses himself:
"Having abandoned all conditioned things, Which consist of immeasurable multitudes of virtuous deeds,
Those who were to be delivered, whether near or far, Have now been delivered."
The venerable Ānanda, his heart struck with alarm and his hair standing on end, hurried to the Buddha. Having prostrated himself, he stood to one side and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How extraordinary, World-Honored One!
"The earth has shaken to such an extent; what are the causes and conditions for this?
The Buddha said to Ānanda, "In general, there are eight causes and conditions for an earthquake in the world."

What are the eight? The earth beneath heaven rests upon water; the water rests upon wind; the wind rests upon space. When a great wind occasionally arises spontaneously within space, the great waters are stirred; when the great waters are stirred, the entire earth quakes. This is the first.

Sometimes a śramaṇa who has attained the Way, or a sublime deva, whose virtue of precepts is most flourishing, desires to test his own power; when he presses down a small portion of the earth with his hand, the entire earth trembles—this is the second [cause].

When the Bodhisattva first descends from the fourth heaven into his mother’s womb, with wisdom and a compassionate mind, desiring to manifest the transformation of the Way and enlighten the ignorant, he emits divine light that shakes heaven and earth, causing Brahmā, Śakra, Māra, śramaṇas, and brahmins alike to behold this radiance; this is the third [sign].
When the Bodhisattva is born from his mother’s womb, his virtue moves the devas; the sky is pure and free from clouds, divine light shines afar, and the entire earth trembles—this is the fourth.

When the Bodhisattva attains the unsurpassed Way and becomes a truly enlightened Buddha, the entire earth shakes greatly and celestial deities spread in the four directions, extolling the name of the Buddha; this is the fifth.

Furthermore, when he has already attained Buddhahood and during his first great assembly, he turns the wheel of the Dharma three times; then gods and humans understand it, these and those bodhisattvas ascend to achieve the Great Way, his radiance shines afar, and at that time the entire earth trembles—this is the sixth.

As his Buddhist teaching was about to end, he wished to relinquish the formations of life and no longer abide in his vitality; thereupon, he emitted a great radiance to exhort and inspire devas and humans, and the entire earth shook—this is the seventh.

As when the Buddha, the One Honored by the Multitudes, was about to relinquish his body and enter parinirvāṇa, there was no place his radiance did not illuminate; when the celestial deities gathered there, the earth shook everywhere—this is the eighth.
Ānanda asked,
"Has the Buddha now relinquished his life-force?
The Buddha said:
"He has already relinquished it. Ānanda said,
"In the past, I heard the Buddha say:"

"If there is a disciple who understands the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), cultivates and practices them extensively, maintains focused mindfulness without forgetfulness, and acts according to his will, he may remain without dying for a kalpa or more."
"Yet the Buddha’s virtue and wisdom surpass these by far; can he not remain for a longer time?
The Buddha replied to Ānanda:
"Now that you have spoken thus, is it not excessive?"
I have spoken to you regarding the four bases of spiritual power (ṛddhipāda) even up to three times;

yet you remain silent, submerged in obscurity, failing to develop clear insight, and being obscured by Māra. How can you claim to possess what the Buddha has taught? Once words are uttered, how could you possibly act contrary to them?
He replied, "No, sir. "So it is, Ānanda!"
"An unwise person, having already spoken, subsequently contradicts himself;
I am not like that.
Ānanda shed tears and said:
"How swift it is! How rapid is the Buddha’s entry into *nirvāṇa*!
The Eye of the World has been extinguished."
At that time, the Buddha instructed the Venerable Ānanda to invite the wandering bhikṣus from the kingdom of Vaiśālī.
Having received these instructions, he immediately invited them, and they all assembled in the lecture hall; having prostrated themselves, they stood to one side.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus: "The world is impermanent; nothing therein is solid or enduring.

All things must eventually disperse, for nothing remains forever. The movements of the mind and consciousness serve only to deceive oneself. As for the union of affection and love, who can maintain it for long? Even heaven and earth and Mount Sumeru shall yet crumble and perish; how much more so for human beings—how could they hope to endure eternally?"
The sorrow and suffering of birth and death are indeed things to be loathed!
Three months from now, the Buddha shall enter *parinirvāṇa*; do not be surprised, and do not grieve.

Furthermore, all Buddhas of the past, future, and present attain [enlightenment] through the Dharma; as long as the teachings of the sutras remain, you should simply exert yourselves, diligently study and practice, and maintain a pure mind. By striving toward liberation, when the activities of the mind and consciousness cease, one neither dies nor is born again, nor does one wander through the five realms of existence, casting off one body only to receive another.
Once the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) have been severed, one is no longer afflicted by hunger, thirst, cold, heat, sorrow, grief, suffering, or distress.

When a person knows how to rectify the mind, all the devas in the heavens rejoice on their behalf. One should subdue the mind, making it supple and self-effacing; do not follow the movements of the mind, for there is nothing the mind will not do. Even the attainment of the Way is a matter of the mind.
The mind creates gods, the mind creates humans, and the mind creates ghosts, spirits, animals, and those in the hells;

all are the workings of the mind. From the activities of the mind arise all phenomena: the mind creates consciousness (*vijñāna*), consciousness creates mentation (*manas*), and mentation turns back into the mind. Of these, the mind is taken as the primary; the mental will constitutes conduct, and conduct constitutes destiny. Whether one is worthy or foolish depends on conduct; whether one lives long or dies young depends on destiny.
Now, will, conduct, and destiny are mutually dependent; whatever good or evil one does, one must personally experience its consequences.

If a father commits an unwholesome act, his son does not suffer in his stead; if a son commits an unwholesome act, his father likewise does not suffer for it. Goodness brings its own blessings, and evil brings its own calamities.

That the Buddha is now revered by all those above and below in heaven and earth is entirely due to his resolve; therefore, one should practice the Dharma with a correct mind. Only those who practice the Dharma can attain rest in the present life and find peace in the present life. You should properly grasp, uphold, receive, recite, and contemplate it with a tranquil mind. In this way, my pure Dharma may endure for a long time, and you may compassionately deliver the world from its manifold sufferings, bringing benefit, peace, and tranquility to all devas and humans.
“Bhikṣus, you should know!
What is the Dharma?

It refers to the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the four dhyāna practices, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path. By receiving and practicing these as they are, one may attain liberation and ensure that the Dharma does not decline.”
"What are the four foundations of mindfulness? They are:

contemplating the body as the body internally, contemplating the body as the body externally, and contemplating the body both internally and externally, reflecting with discernment to sever delusion and confusion;
contemplating feelings, the mind, and phenomena, all as previously described."
"What are the four bases of mental power?
To immediately sever evil states that have already arisen through the diligence of self-mastery and the internalization of the basis of mental power;
to restrain and prevent unarisen evil states from arising through the diligence of self-mastery and the internalization of the basis of mental power;..."
Regarding wholesome states not yet arisen, one is able to bring them forth; this is diligence of the nature of cultivation, characterized by self-restraint and rectitude of mind.

Regarding wholesome states already arisen, one establishes the will so as not to forget them, enabling them to increase further; this is diligence of the nature of intention, characterized by rectitude of mind.
“What are the four bases of spiritual power? They are:

the base of spiritual power consisting of concentration of intention accompanied by the thought of desire, which, through the cessation of all conditioned activities, is endowed with mindfulness; in this, one’s desire is not perverse, one neither grasps nor rejects, and one constantly maintains pure conduct.

The same applies to the base of spiritual power consisting of concentration of energy, the base of spiritual power consisting of concentration of mind, and the base of spiritual power consisting of concentration of investigation—all are identical, as explained in the preceding text.”
"What are the four dhyānas?
Abandoning unwholesome states of desire, one dwells in pure mindfulness and conduct, with the mind delighting in non-action; this constitutes the practice of the first dhyāna.
When mindfulness and conduct have ceased, one maintains internal one-pointedness of mind, with the mind set upon tranquility; this constitutes the practice of the second dhyāna."
Contemplating only the absence of lust, the mind is at peace and the body upright; discerning and seeing the truth, one accomplishes the practice of the third dhyāna.
Having already severed both suffering and pleasure, and being free from the perceptions of sorrow and joy, the mind is utterly pure, and one accomplishes the practice of the fourth dhyāna.
"What are the five faculties?
First is the faculty of faith, which inclines the mind toward the four bases of joy;
second is the faculty of diligence, which rectifies the four bases of mindfulness."
Third is the faculty of mindfulness, which keeps the four applications of mindfulness in mind;
fourth is the faculty of concentration, which contemplates the practices of the four dhyānas;
fifth is the faculty of wisdom, which perceives the four noble truths.
"What are the five powers?
First is the power of faith, whereby the joyful mind is indestructible;
second is the power of diligence, whereby one is always able to exercise firm self-mastery."
Third is the power of mindfulness, whereby one attains the will for contemplation;
fourth is the power of concentration, whereby the mind of dhyāna remains undisturbed;
fifth is the power of wisdom, whereby one realizes the Way through self-attestation.
"What are the seven factors of enlightenment?

They are the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness, the factor of enlightenment of dharma-discernment, the factor of enlightenment of energy, the factor of enlightenment of rapture, the factor of enlightenment of tranquility, the factor of enlightenment of concentration, and the factor of enlightenment of equanimity."
“What is called the Eightfold Path?

Right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration—these are the dharmas for crossing over the world and attaining purity. At that time, the Buddha invited the Venerable Ānanda to go together to the town of Kuraraghara, and he immediately accepted the instruction and set out.
The Buddha, delighting in Vaiśālī, passed through the kingdom and emerged from the city gate; he turned his body to the right, looked back at the gate, and smiled.
The Venerable Ānanda immediately adjusted his robes, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and asked:
"Since I have served you for more than twenty years, I have never seen the Buddha travel without a specific cause."
“When you turned your body to look at the gate and smiled, what was the cause and condition for this?
The Buddha said, “It is so, it is so.”
"Ānanda!
It is not the custom of the Buddha to turn his body away or smile in vain.
This is my final sight of Vaiśālī; therefore, I looked upon it and smiled."
Thereupon the Buddha himself recited these verses:
"This is my final time To travel and observe in Vaiśālī;
I am about to travel toward Nirvāṇa, And shall no longer receive a physical body."
Another bhikṣu also praised him in verse:
“The Buddha declared this to be his final [existence]; his bodily conduct has reached its ultimate limit here.
If he should now sink into the pure void, where shall we behold the arrival of the Sage?”
The Buddha, together with Ānanda, went to the northern forest grove north of the town of Kuraraghara and addressed the bhikṣus:
“You should guard the pure precepts, you should contemplate meditative concentration, and you should understand wisdom.”

Now, one who maintains the precepts and possesses concentration and wisdom achieves great virtue and attains abundant renown; they are forever freed from greed, lust, anger, and delusion, and may become an Arhat. Those who desire to attain perfect liberation in this very life should apply themselves to self-understanding, so as to bring this birth to its end and enter the path of purity.
"Having already practiced as was appropriate, I now know my own body and shall not receive another in the future.
The Buddha again requested the worthy Ānanda to go together to the town of Kaccāna, where they stayed beneath a tree to the north of the city.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
“You should maintain pure precepts, cultivate meditative concentration, and seek to realize wisdom.

One who maintains pure precepts does not follow the three states; one whose mind is concentrated does not allow it to be distracted; and one who has realized wisdom abandons the grasping for desires and acts without obstruction.”
Possessing precepts, concentration, and wisdom, with great virtue and abundant renown, and further having abandoned the three impurities, one will ultimately attain arhatship.
If you wish to achieve perfect liberation with this very body, you should diligently seek the truth so that this life may be brought to an end and you enter the path of purity.
"By practicing as it should be practiced, one will know for oneself the cessation [of suffering], and shall not undergo further rebirth.
The Buddha, together with Ānanda, passed through the towns of Yamunā, Suvarṇabhūmi, Hastigrāma, and Puṣpapura, until they reached the town of Śubhapura.
In various places, he taught these three essentials to his disciples, saying:
"One should guard the precepts, cultivate meditative concentration, and understand wisdom.
By maintaining these three, one's virtue becomes abundant and one's reputation great; one eliminates lust, anger, and delusion—this is called the Right Crossing."

Once the mind of ethical discipline is established, the mind of concentration is accomplished; once the mind of concentration is accomplished, the mind of wisdom becomes clear. Just as a clean and pure cloth takes on colors clearly and beautifully, when these three minds are present, the Path is easily attained. One should simply focus the mind with diligence of body to seek liberation, so that this life may be brought to an end and one may enter into purity.
One who practices according to what is appropriate knows for themselves that this is the limit and will no longer undergo rebirth.

If one is unable to fully cultivate the practices of precept, concentration, and wisdom yet desires to transcend the hardships of the world, these three qualities will cause the mind to open and resolve itself;

sitting in contemplation, one then clearly perceives the five destinies—heavenly beings, humans, hell-dwellers, animals, and spirits—and fully knows the intentions and thoughts of all sentient beings.
For example, when the water of a mountain stream is clear, all the pebbles within it—whether blue, yellow, white, or black—are visible;
so too, because the mind of one who has attained the Way is pure, everything they behold is clearly seen. Those who wish to attain the Way should purify their inner minds.
Just as when water is turbid, nothing can be seen, so too if the mind is impure, one cannot transcend the world.

What the teacher perceives and proclaims, the disciple should practice; yet if what the teacher has realized does not enter the disciple’s heart, one must rectify one's thoughts. When the intention of one's thoughts is upright, the Way will be attained of its own accord.
The Buddha, having already delighted in the sublime purity, further invited the Venerable Ānanda to go together to the town of Venuyāya, where they stayed beneath a tree to the north of the city.
At the hour of *prahara*, Ānanda rose from his meditation, went to where the Buddha was, and after prostrating himself, joined his palms and asked:
"I wish to know, in brief, how many causes there are for an earthquake?"
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
“There are three causes and conditions:
first, the earth rests upon water; water rests upon wind; and wind rests upon space. When a great wind arises, the water is disturbed; when the water is disturbed, the earth shakes.”
Second, for the sake of the śramaṇas who have attained the Way and the wondrous devas, the earth shakes so as to manifest a spiritual response.

Third, it is by the power of the Buddha; since my attainment of Buddhahood, the earth has already shaken before and after, such that throughout the three thousand suns and moons and the twelve thousand heavens and earths, there is none that is not moved and inspired, and many among the devas, humans, ghosts, and spirits gain hearing and understanding.
Ānanda sighed in admiration and said:
"How marvelous!
The Buddha is peerless; through the natural Dharma, there is nothing he cannot move. His supreme virtue and supreme Way are so sublime and majestic."
The Buddha said: "So it is,
so it is, Ānanda!"

The Buddha’s virtue is not small; rather, having accumulated merit over countless kalpas and practiced all manner of goodness, he has attained Buddhahood by himself. Possessing such wondrous and spontaneous Dharma-transformations, he knows all and sees all, with nothing that he does not penetrate and nothing that he does not transform.

I recall that in the past, with a heart of loving-kindness and compassion, I transformed and met with hundreds of thousands of people, including the kings and gentlemen of the world; according to their respective appearances, I comforted them by preaching the Way of the Sūtras, circulating my teachings everywhere to lead them toward wholesome intentions.

Manifesting such transformations throughout the eight directions, he accords with the local customs, dress, and languages of each land; observing what dharma each person practices and which sutras they know, he expounds and bestows upon them the Right Path. For those who delight in the meaning of words, he provides the formal teachings; for those who understand principles, he explains the supreme essentials. Having firmly established their resolve, he then vanishes.

Even if kings and gentlemen did not know who I was at first, they later all came to savor its flavor and reverently receive the transformation of the Dharma; this is the pure, subtle, and spontaneous Dharma of the Buddha.
"Furthermore, Ānanda!..."

Having attained the power of the Buddha to enter everywhere and manifest transformations through the ritual methods of a Buddha, he entered the assembly of śramaṇas to serve as their teacher and guide; thereafter, he transformed his appearance and entered the assembly of brahmins.

Furthermore, householders and scholars of various schools, according to their respective dress, accents, and languages, are granted the teachings of the Way and achieve all success; yet these become erroneous and perverse dharmas. Once they have passed away, their descendants all receive my teaching but do not recognize me—this is the rare and spontaneous dharma of the Buddha.

The Buddha likewise ascended to the first level, the Heaven of the Four Great Kings; he ascended throughout the second, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; the third, the Yāma Heaven; the fourth, the Tuṣita Heaven; the fifth, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven; and the sixth, the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, pervading the realm of Māra.

Furthermore, ascending to the seventh, the Brahmakāyika Heaven; the eighth, the Brahmapurohita Heaven; the ninth, the Mahābrahmā Heaven; the tenth, the Ābhāsvara Heaven; the eleventh, the Parīttābha Heaven; the twelfth, the Apramāṇābha Heaven; the thirteenth, the Ābhāsvarābha Heaven; the fourteenth, the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven; the fifteenth, the Parīttaśubha Heaven; the sixteenth, the Apramāṇaśubha Heaven; the seventeenth, the Śubhakṛtsnābha Heaven; the eighteenth, the Puṇyaprasava Heaven; the nineteenth, the Bṛhatphala Heaven; the twentieth, the Abṛha Heaven; the twenty-first, the Atapa Heaven; the twenty-second, the Sudṛśa Heaven; the twenty-third, the Sudarśana Heaven; and the twenty-fourth, the Avṛha Heaven—I have pervaded all these realms with hundreds of thousands of people.
