Once the enshrinement in the treasury had been completed and the various incenses piled up, the minister Uṣa took up fire intending to ignite the Buddha; yet as soon as the fire reached the pile, it was extinguished, and though he approached three times, it would not burn.
The worthy Aniruddha said to Ānanda:
"The reason the fire does not burn is due to the intention of the devas.

They see that Mahākāśyapa, leading a multitude of five hundred followers, is coming from Pāpīyas and is already halfway there; because they wish for him to pay homage to the Buddha in person, they have caused the fire not to ignite."
Ānanda said:
“Yes. I respectfully accept as you wish.”

At that time, there was a certain ascetic named Āyīwéi who, having seen the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, obtained divine māndārava flowers. While he was on his way, half-way along the road, Kāśyapa saw him, approached his carriage, and asked:
"Do you know my venerable teacher, the Buddha?"
He immediately replied:
"I know it; he entered parinirvāṇa seven days ago. Gods and humans have gathered everywhere to make offerings to his body. I have come from there and obtained these celestial flowers."
Thereupon, Kāśyapa was despondent and unhappy.
Among the five hundred bhikṣus, some wandered about in agitation, looking up to heaven and crying out in grievance:
"The Buddha’s parinirvāṇa—how sudden and swift it is!"
"The Eye of the World has been extinguished.
Within him there was grief, lamentation, and sorrow; he reflected upon the suffering of the world, bound by the ties of affection, and failed to see this Path.
Kāśyapa spoke to enlighten him:

"O worthy ones, cast off your grief! You should know that this body arises entirely from conditions; the mind acts and acts again, leading to impermanence and suffering. Those who are born must die, and death is followed by birth; there is no peace in the five realms of existence, only the bliss of Nirvana."

"Those who have not yet attained the Way should seek the benefit of the Dharma; by abandoning conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) and ceasing all attachments, one shall attain it. Girding our robes, let us go quickly, and we shall behold the Buddha’s body.
Among the assembly was one named Dhanyaka, also a son of the Śākya clan who had gone forth together with the Buddha.
He addressed the bhikṣus, saying: "Why do you worry further? From this day forward, we have attained self-mastery. That old man always says:"
"One should practice this; one should not practice that.
Now, has he not passed away and gone far beyond?
Kāśyapa was displeased.
Having traveled to the twin trees and reached where the Buddha’s remains lay, he said to Ānanda,
"Before the cremation takes place, I beg to see the Buddha's body.
Ānanda replied:

"The Buddha's body has already been wrapped and saturated with sesame oil, enshrined within a golden coffin, and covered externally with a mass of various fragrances; though the cremation has not yet occurred, it is already difficult to behold."
Kāśyapa requested this up to three times, but Ānanda answered as he had before, for he considered that it would be difficult to behold the Buddha’s body again.

Thereupon, the Buddha’s remains extended both feet out from within the nested coffins; all who saw this were filled with joy. Kāśyapa prostrated himself in worship, and seeing a strange color upon the Buddha’s feet, he looked up and asked Ānanda:
“The Buddha’s body was golden in color; what is the reason for this difference?”
Ānanda replied, “There was a frail old woman who prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and shed tears upon them; that is why they appear different in color.
Mahākāśyapa was again displeased and sighed as he uttered this eulogy:
"He acts for the cessation of non-arising, so as not to undergo old age and death again;
he acts so as not to meet [them] again, and thus there is no encounter with what is loathed.
Having already abandoned affection and love, he does not suffer the grief of separation."
One should seek skillful means to bring about this state.
For the Buddha, the five aggregates are purified; having been severed, they do not arise again.
Furthermore, he does not act for the sake of action, yet there is the experience of these five aggregates.
Suffering has been completely exhausted, and its root has also been removed;
one should diligently seek skillful means to attain such peace.
The Buddha has severed the world; he is fully liberated from all craving and desire.
Furthermore, by being able to endure all things, one attains freedom from all calamities and hardships.
For the sake of one's own peace and security, and to bring peace to the world as well, one should prostrate before this [Dharma];
thus shall one forever attain deliverance across the three realms.
The sūtras and precepts spoken by the Buddha are the most luminous in the world;
having extensively manifested the Right Path, they are examined with certainty and free from doubt.
They also pervade the whole world, enabling all to transcend old age and death.
Among all those who encounter a Buddha, who would not receive his vast grace?
Like the moon illuminating the night to dispel the gloom of darkness,
or like the sun shining during the day, enabling the world to be bright.
Just as a flash of lightning appears, momentarily illuminating thick clouds,
so the Buddha’s radiance emerges for an instant, completely illuminating the three realms.
Of all rivers that exist by name, none surpasses the Kunlun River.
All things are called "great waters," yet they are also the ocean beyond fault.
Among all the constellations, the moon is the foremost in brilliance;
the Buddha is the guide of the world, the Honored One above and below heaven.
The reason the Buddha has crossed over the world is that his bestowal of merit is now complete;
the teachings and precepts he has proclaimed are clear and distinct in every place.
Furthermore, through the dissemination of the Dharma, his disciples joyfully accept and practice them.
"May devas, humans, ghosts, and spirits, as well as nāgas, respectfully receive and practice this rite.
Having spoken thus, Kāśyapa bowed his head at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated the funeral pyre three times, and withdrew to stand to one side.

The bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, as well as the devas, nāgas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas, each came forward, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated the funeral pyre three times, and stood to one side.
Thereupon, the Buddha’s body was consumed by fire spontaneously without being ignited.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda spoke these verses:
“The Buddha, with inner and outer purity, Has become a body of the Brahma-world.”
The spirit of this vehicle descends, and now it is applied here.
Wrapped in brocade and fine cotton a thousand times over, yet not used to clothe the body,
nor even washed, it remains as pure and bright as ever.
When the night had ended and the Buddha’s body was completely consumed by the fire, four trees spontaneously grew from the site:
the *sūcīnī* tree, the *kāyasthā* tree, the *aśvattha* tree, and the *nyagrodha* tree.

The prominent clans of the kingdom together inspected the Buddha’s relics, filling a golden urn with them. They placed it upon a palanquin and carried it into the city, setting it upon the high altar in the great hall; there they performed music, scattered flowers, burned incense, and paid their respects through offerings.

At that time, the Kshatriyas of the kingdom of Pāpīyan, the Kulinas of the kingdom of Kaṃbala, the Mālavas of the kingdom of Aṅga, the Brahmins of the kingdom of Jambudvīpa, and the Licchavis of the kingdom of Vaiśālī, hearing that the Buddha had stayed at the twin trees and entered *parinirvāṇa*, each prepared the fourfold army—elephant troops, cavalry, chariot troops, and infantry—and arrived outside the city of Kuśinagara. They dispatched an envoy with these words:

"We have heard that the Buddha, the Great Benefactor, has stayed here and passed into extinction. He was our teacher as well; out of a heart of reverence and longing, we have all come to you to request a portion of the Buddha’s relics, wishing to return to our respective homelands to erect stūpas and temples."
King Kauśāmbī said, "The Buddha came here himself;
I shall provide for him. You have troubled me from afar, so you shall not obtain a portion of the relics.
The Śākyas of the country of Rakta-saras also arrayed their fourfold army and arrived, reporting: [that they too would provide for the Buddha].

"Having heard that the Buddha, the One of Many Blessings, has entered parinirvāṇa here, and that this Sage Hero of the Śākyas was born from our own kin—indeed, our own father—we have come with hearts of reverence and longing to request a portion of his relics so that we may establish a stūpa and temple in our own land."
The King replied as before, refusing to share a portion.
King Ajātaśatru of Magadha again arrayed his fourfold army and crossed the river ferry to come, sending the Brahmin Māṭa to inquire after news and convey these earnest words:

"In former times, I harbored a heart of faith and was your friend; we were without contention or dispute. Now the Buddha, the Most Honored One, has entered parinirvāṇa here; he is the Honored One of the Three Realms and truly my own deity. With a heart of deep veneration and longing, I have come to request a portion of the relics. You should grant them to me, and I shall give you all my precious treasures; I pray that we may share them together until the end."
The King replied, "The Buddha will come here himself; I shall provide for him. Thank you, Great King, but a share of the relics cannot be obtained.
Thereupon, Maugalyāyana gathered the multitude and, composing a verse, addressed them, saying:
"Now each has composed themselves, coming from afar to prostrate;
with humility they seek their portion.
Their movements stir the multitude, for the fourfold army is here."
"If your arguments are not accepted, you shall certainly be brought down by our arguments.
The people of Kauśāmbī also replied in verse:
"We have traveled far to trouble you, and we have humbled ourselves to pay our respects."
The Buddha came to leave behind his physical form, yet we did not dare grant him our permission.
If you wish to lead the entire assembly, we likewise possess such means;
if you command us all to descend together, then there shall be no cause for fear.
The Brahmin Maokuei (Maukṣya) addressed the crowd, saying:
"Gentlemen, you have all long since received the Buddha’s solemn teachings, reciting his words daily and submitting your hearts to his benevolent transformation.

Since you desire the peace of all sentient beings, and because the Buddha’s great compassion has led us to burn his body and preserve his relics in order to widely benefit the world, why should we now destroy our original intention of grace? The śarīra are already here; we need only divide them."
The assembly all acclaimed this as excellent. They all went to the śarīra, bowed their heads in prostration, and stood to one side. They then commissioned Moke to divide it.
Thereupon, Moke took a jar about the capacity of one *shi*, coated its interior with honey, divided the relics into eight portions, and addressed the assembly, saying:
"I already revere the Buddha, and I also admire the intentions of the assembly; I wish to place these relics in my jar and return to build a stūpa."
They all said, "How wise! This is indeed knowing the proper time," and they immediately agreed to grant it.
There was also a brahmin named Uruvilvā who addressed the crowd, saying, "I secretly admire your noble intention;
I beg for the charred coals of the ground so that I may return and erect a stūpa there."
They all agreed to give it to him.
Later, a foreign master from the state of Heng obtained some of the ground ash.
At that time, the eight kingdoms had each received one of the eight portions of the Buddha’s relics and returned home to erect stupas, all of which were exceedingly magnificent and beautiful.

The Brahmin Moke, the Daoist Daren Dui of Zhongyi, and the Daoist De Digui of Hengguo all returned to their respective villages—Bebi and others—and upon their return, they all erected stūpas and temples.
There are eight stupas for the eight portions of the Śarīra; the ninth is the Jar Stupa, the tenth is the Charcoal Stupa, and the eleventh is the Ash Stupa.

The Buddha was born on the eighth day of the fourth month, he left home on the eighth day of the fourth month, he attained the Way of Buddhahood on the eighth day of the fourth month, and he entered Parinirvāṇa on the eighth day of the fourth month—all occurring when the Buddha Star appeared. At this time, the flowers and blossoms of the hundred grasses bloom and the trees flourish in abundance.
The Buddha had already entered parinirvāṇa, and the light of the world was extinguished; the devas of the ten directions all turned themselves toward the Buddha for refuge.

Once the śarīra had been divided, because the fourfold assembly from distant regions had not yet heard the news in its entirety, he remained for ninety days before the stūpas and temples were erected.
All the visiting kings, noble families, commoners, their households, and their servants observed the *upavāsa* fast for ninety days.
In a distant land, the fourfold assembly of disciples gathered together in Kauśāmbī and asked Ānanda:
"Where should a stūpa be erected?
Ānanda replied:
"When you have gone forty *li* outside the city, you shall construct a stūpa and temple at the crossroads of Weizhi Village.

The prominent clans of Kauśāmbī collectively fashioned bricks of baked clay, three feet in length and breadth, which they assembled to build a stūpa. Its height and its dimensions were both one and a half *zhang*. Within it, they enshrined golden urns containing the *śarīra* relics. They erected a tall pillar and a wheel of Dharma, hung silk banners from the canopy, and offered worship and offerings with lamps, flowers, incense, and music. Thus, the people of the entire nation were able to together generate merit.
Mahākāśyapa, Aniruddha, and the assembly of bhikṣus deliberated together:

"The thirty thousand people in a single day, along with the eminent families and ministers of various kingdoms, having encountered the Buddha, shall practice merit with reverent intent; in the end, they will all be reborn in the fourth heaven and meet Maitreya to attain liberation."

The King of Kauśāmbī shall be reborn in the twelfth heaven, the Water-Sound Heaven; when Maitreya attains Buddhahood, he shall descend to build a vihāra for the Buddha that will surpass the present Jetavana Garden.
Ānanda asked Mahākāśyapa:
"Why did King Kṛkin not seek the path of arhatship under Maitreya Buddha?
He replied:
"Because this king has not yet grown weary of the suffering of birth and death, and one who is not weary of suffering cannot attain the state of an Arhat.
Ānanda said, "I am already weary of the suffering of the body; yet I have not been able to leave the world—how is it that I do not attain the Way?"
Kāśyapa replied:

“You merely maintain the precepts but do not practice the contemplation of the body; you sit leaning upon the notion of food within the cycle of birth and death, and because your activities within birth and death have not yet ceased.”
When the ninety days had passed, Mahākāśyapa, Aniruddha, and the assembly of bhikṣus held a consultation together:

"The Buddha’s twelvefold scriptures comprise the four Āgamas. Since Ānanda alone has attended upon the Buddha for so long, he has memorized everything the Buddha taught; we should receive them from him in writing. However, we fear that he has not yet attained the Way and may still harbor worldly desires. We wish to challenge Ānanda regarding past events by arranging a high seat for him, making him ascend it three times and descend it three times; in this way, we may obtain the truth."
They all replied, "Very well.

Once the assembly was seated, the *vaiyāvṛtyakara* bhikṣu escorted Ānanda out; after a short while, he invited him back in. When Ānanda entered and paid homage to the Saṃgha, those who had not yet attained the Path all rose for him.
The bhikṣu in charge of affairs sat upon the high seat in the center; thereupon, he yielded it, saying:
"This is not Ānanda’s seat.
The assembly of bhikṣus said:
"Because you have mastered the Buddha's sutras, we have invited you to this high seat; we wish to ask you something.
Ānanda took his seat.
The assembly of monks then asked:
"You have committed a great transgression; do you not know it yourself?
Formerly, the Buddha said:
'Jambudvīpa is a place of joy.'"
"Why do you not answer?
The bhikṣu in charge of affairs commanded Ānanda to descend.
He immediately descended and replied:
“Does the Buddha lack self-mastery that he must require my words?
The assembly of monks remained silent.
The *vaiyāvṛtyakara* bhikṣu then again directed Ānanda to ascend.
The assembly asked again:
"The Buddha has told you:
'One who attains the foundation of the four dhyānas may remain for one kalpa or more.'"
"Why do you remain silent?
Ānanda replied, "The Buddha has said that Maitreya shall descend to become a Buddha; those who have first entered the Dharma should achieve their realization through him."
"If you were to remain yourself, how would that differ from Maitreya?
The monks again remained silent.
Ānanda was struck with fear, and the bhikṣus said:
"The wise one should explain the Buddha’s sūtras in accordance with the Dharma and its meaning.
He replied, "So be it."
Thus he ascended [the hall] three times, and when Ānanda finally ascended and said,
"I have heard thus at one time," those among the assembly who had not yet attained the Way all wept and said,
"The Buddha has just finished preaching the sutra; why is he now so ill?"
Mahākāśyapa then selected forty arhats from among the assembly to receive the four Āgamas from Ānanda:
first, the Madhyama-āgama; second, the Dīrgha-āgama; third, the Ekottara-āgama; and fourth, the Saṃyukta-āgama.

These four types of writings are: first, those produced by lust; second, those produced by anger and joy; third, those produced by ignorance; and fourth, those produced by lack of filial piety and failure to respect teachers.
The texts of the four Āgamas each occupied sixty rolls of silk.
The bhikṣus said:
"We shall use these to transcribe the four texts so that they may be propagated throughout the world."

Therefore, at the site where the Buddha was cremated, four trees grew spontaneously. Consequently, they collected his remains and separately transcribed the twelve divisions of the Buddha’s scriptures.

When the period of one thousand years has elapsed, those who have upheld the Buddha’s sutras and precepts shall all subsequently be reborn in the presence of Maitreya Buddha, where they shall attain liberation from the cycle of birth and death.
